title: Counting and Totals
summary: Summarize many rows into one with count, sum, avg, min, and max.
intro: How many orders came in, and how much were they worth? Aggregate functions answer questions like these by turning many rows into a single row of totals.
setup:
CREATE TABLE orders (
    id integer,
    customer text,
    status text,
    total numeric(10, 2),
    coupon text,
    ordered_on date
);
INSERT INTO orders (id, customer, status, total, coupon, ordered_on) VALUES
    (1, 'Ana', 'pending', 42.50, 'SAVE10', DATE '2025-03-01'),
    (2, 'Ben', 'shipped', 18.00, NULL, DATE '2025-03-02'),
    (3, 'Ana', 'delivered', 65.25, NULL, DATE '2025-03-03'),
    (4, 'Chloe', 'delivered', 120.00, 'SPRING', DATE '2025-03-05'),
    (5, 'Dev', 'cancelled', 30.00, NULL, DATE '2025-03-06'),
    (6, 'Ben', 'delivered', 9.99, 'SAVE10', DATE '2025-03-08'),
    (7, 'Eva', 'pending', 75.00, NULL, DATE '2025-03-09'),
    (8, 'Chloe', 'shipped', 54.40, NULL, DATE '2025-03-10'),
    (9, 'Ana', 'cancelled', 22.10, 'SPRING', DATE '2025-03-12'),
    (10, 'Femi', 'delivered', 47.80, NULL, DATE '2025-03-14');

steps.title: Counting rows
steps.body:
An aggregate function reads many rows and returns one value. This lesson uses an `orders` table:

```sql harness
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS orders CASCADE;
{{code}}
```

```sql
CREATE TABLE orders (id integer, customer text, status text,
    total numeric(10, 2), coupon text, ordered_on date);
```

| id | customer | status | total | coupon | ordered_on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Ana | pending | 42.50 | SAVE10 | 2025-03-01 |
| 2 | Ben | shipped | 18.00 | NULL | 2025-03-02 |
| 3 | Ana | delivered | 65.25 | NULL | 2025-03-03 |

It has 10 orders with the statuses pending, shipped, delivered, and cancelled. Some coupons are `NULL`.

`count` comes in three forms, and each answers a different question:

```sql
SELECT
    count(*),                 -- how many rows
    count(coupon),            -- how many rows where coupon is not NULL
    count(DISTINCT customer)  -- how many different customers, NULL not included
FROM orders;
```

The query returns one row no matter how many rows it read. On an empty table every `count` is `0`, never `NULL`.

example.title: Order counts
example.prompt: Count the orders, the orders that used a coupon, and the different customers.
example.code:
SELECT
    count(*) AS orders,
    count(coupon) AS with_coupon,
    count(DISTINCT customer) AS customers
FROM orders;
example.explanation: `count(*)` counts all 10 rows. `count(coupon)` skips the 6 rows where `coupon` is `NULL`, leaving 4. `count(DISTINCT customer)` counts Ana, Ben, Chloe, Dev, Eva, and Femi once each, even though Ana has three orders.

practice.title: Statuses and coupon codes
practice.prompt:
Count the orders, how many different statuses they have, and how many different coupon codes were used.

1. Select from `orders` and return one row.
2. Name the row count `orders`.
3. Name the number of different `status` values `statuses`.
4. Name the number of different `coupon` values `coupon_codes`. Missing coupons must not count.

Expected output:

```text
 orders | statuses | coupon_codes
--------+----------+--------------
     10 |        4 |            2
(1 row)
```
practice.starter:
SELECT
    count(*) AS orders
    -- TODO: add the statuses and coupon_codes counts
FROM orders;
practice.solution:
SELECT
    count(*) AS orders,
    count(DISTINCT status) AS statuses,
    count(DISTINCT coupon) AS coupon_codes
FROM orders;

tests.stdin:
INSERT INTO orders (id, customer, status, total, coupon, ordered_on) VALUES
    (11, 'Gus', 'returned', 15.00, 'WELCOME', DATE '2025-03-15'),
    (12, 'Ana', 'pending', 33.00, 'SAVE10', DATE '2025-03-16'),
    (13, 'Hana', 'pending', 12.75, NULL, DATE '2025-03-17');

hints: Add each count as its own column, separated by a comma.
To count different values, put `DISTINCT` inside the parentheses, right before the column name.
Counting distinct coupons already skips `NULL`, so no `WHERE` is needed.

steps.title: Sum, average, smallest, largest
steps.body:
`sum`, `avg`, `min`, and `max` work like `count`: many rows in, one value out. All of them skip `NULL` values.

```sql
SELECT sum(total), round(avg(total), 2), min(total), max(total) FROM orders;
```

`avg` of a numeric column prints many digits, so wrap it in `round(x, 2)`. `min` and `max` work on numbers, text, and dates. `max(ordered_on)` is the latest date.

Add `WHERE` and the aggregates only see the rows it keeps. The filter runs first, then the summary. That order is why an aggregate cannot go inside `WHERE`.

A plain column next to an aggregate is an error too, because one summary row cannot show every customer. Getting one row per customer takes `GROUP BY`, which comes next. Try this in the editor:

```sql error
SELECT customer, count(*) FROM orders;
```

```text
ERROR:  column "orders.customer" must appear in the GROUP BY clause or be used in an aggregate function
```

The gotcha: when no rows are left, `count(*)` is `0` but `sum`, `avg`, `min`, and `max` are `NULL`, which prints as a blank:

```sql
SELECT count(*), sum(total)
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'returned';
```

```text
 count | sum
-------+-----
     0 |
(1 row)
```

If you want `0` instead, write `coalesce(sum(total), 0)`.

example.title: Revenue from orders not cancelled
example.prompt: Total, average, smallest total, and latest order date over every order that was not cancelled.
example.code:
SELECT
    sum(total) AS revenue,
    round(avg(total), 2) AS average,
    min(total) AS smallest,
    max(ordered_on) AS latest
FROM orders
WHERE status <> 'cancelled';
example.explanation: `WHERE` drops the 2 cancelled orders first, so every aggregate reads the other 8. `sum` adds their totals, `avg` divides that by 8 and `round` keeps 2 decimals, `min` picks the smallest total, and `max` on a date column picks the latest date.

practice.title: Delivered order summary
practice.prompt:
Summarize the delivered orders in one row.

1. Keep only orders whose `status` is `'delivered'`.
2. Name the sum of `total` `revenue`.
3. Name the average `total`, rounded to 2 decimal places, `average`.
4. Name the largest `total` `largest`.
5. Name the earliest `ordered_on` date `earliest`.

Expected output:

```text
 revenue | average | largest |  earliest
---------+---------+---------+------------
  243.04 |   60.76 |  120.00 | 2025-03-03
(1 row)
```
practice.starter:
SELECT
    sum(total) AS revenue
    -- TODO: add average, largest, and earliest
FROM orders
-- TODO: add a WHERE that keeps only delivered orders
;
practice.solution:
SELECT
    sum(total) AS revenue,
    round(avg(total), 2) AS average,
    max(total) AS largest,
    min(ordered_on) AS earliest
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'delivered';

tests.stdin: UPDATE orders SET status = 'shipped' WHERE status = 'delivered';

hints: Start from the example's query and change the `WHERE` condition.
Largest means the biggest value and earliest means the smallest date. `min` and `max` work on dates too.
With no delivered orders, every value is `NULL` and prints as a blank. That is correct.

steps.title: Several counts at once with FILTER
steps.body:
`WHERE` filters rows for the whole query, so it can only give one count. To count several groups in a single row, attach a filter to each aggregate with `FILTER (WHERE condition)`:

```sql harness
SELECT
    {{code}}
FROM orders;
```

```sql
count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'pending') AS pending
```

Each aggregate sees only the rows its own filter keeps. Aggregates without a filter still see every row, or every row `WHERE` keeps if the query has one. You can mix filtered and plain aggregates in one `SELECT`, and use `FILTER` with any aggregate, like `sum` or `avg`.

The same rules hold inside a filter: when no rows match, `count` gives `0` and `sum` gives `NULL`.

Older code often writes `sum(CASE WHEN status = 'pending' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` for the same count. It works, but `FILTER` is shorter and says what it means.

example.title: Order board
example.prompt: Count pending and shipped orders, and add up the totals of orders that used a coupon, all in one row.
example.code:
SELECT
    count(*) AS all_orders,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'pending') AS pending,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'shipped') AS shipped,
    sum(total) FILTER (WHERE coupon IS NOT NULL) AS coupon_revenue
FROM orders;
example.explanation: `all_orders` has no filter, so it counts all 10 rows. Each `FILTER` narrows only its own aggregate: 2 orders are pending, 2 are shipped, and the 4 orders with a coupon add up to 194.59.

practice.title: Delivered versus cancelled
practice.prompt:
Report delivered and cancelled orders side by side in one row.

1. Select from `orders` with no `WHERE`.
2. Name the count of orders with `status` `'delivered'` `delivered`.
3. Name the count of orders with `status` `'cancelled'` `cancelled`.
4. Name the sum of `total` over delivered orders `delivered_revenue`.

Expected output:

```text
 delivered | cancelled | delivered_revenue
-----------+-----------+-------------------
         4 |         2 |            243.04
(1 row)
```
practice.starter:
SELECT
    count(*) AS orders
    -- TODO: replace with the delivered, cancelled, and delivered_revenue columns
FROM orders;
practice.solution:
SELECT
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'delivered') AS delivered,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'cancelled') AS cancelled,
    sum(total) FILTER (WHERE status = 'delivered') AS delivered_revenue
FROM orders;

tests.stdin:
UPDATE orders SET status = 'cancelled' WHERE id IN (7, 8);
UPDATE orders SET status = 'delivered' WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE orders SET status = 'pending' WHERE status IN ('delivered', 'cancelled');

hints: Write `FILTER (WHERE ...)` right after each aggregate's closing parenthesis.
`FILTER` works on `sum` the same way it works on `count`. Only the condition decides which totals get added.

recap:
- An aggregate reads many rows and returns one value.
- `count(*)` counts rows, `count(column)` skips `NULL`, and `count(DISTINCT column)` counts different values.
- `sum`, `avg`, `min`, and `max` skip `NULL`. Round averages with `round(avg(x), 2)`.
- `min` and `max` work on numbers, text, and dates.
- `WHERE` runs first, so aggregates only see the rows it keeps, and an aggregate cannot go inside `WHERE`.
- With no rows, `count` is `0` but `sum`, `avg`, `min`, and `max` are `NULL`.
- `aggregate FILTER (WHERE condition)` gives each aggregate its own filter, so one row can hold several counts.
